name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 12 September 1970

clue.text: Filled by gatherings of the absent-minded in the upper house?

definitions.text: Filled by gatherings of the absent-minded in the upper house?

blocks.clueFragment: Filled by gatherings of the absent-minded
blocks.note: surface reading: something packed with the daydreams of forgetful people
setter's reading: the stuffed seat of the Lord Speaker in the House of Lords, packed with a sheep's fleece product

explanation.surface: A wry jibe that the House of Lords is stuffed with daydreaming peers.
explanation.walkthrough: The WOOLSACK is the wool-stuffed seat of the presiding officer in the House of Lords; 'wool-gathering' means daydreaming, so the gatherings of the absent-minded are literally wool.
explanation.definitionFit: The seat stuffed with fleece sits in Britain's upper chamber, the House of Lords, so it is filled with gathered wool.

clue.text: Trebly sticky?

blocks.note: surface reading: three times as gluey
setter's reading: something made of three sticks, the stumps in cricket, which also completes the phrase 'sticky ...' for an awkward spot

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a WICKET is three upright stumps, so it is 'trebly sticky', having three sticks; a 'sticky wicket' is also a difficult situation.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket wicket consists of three wooden stumps, so the thing is made of sticks three times over.

clue.text: "Or emptied some dull — to the drains" (Keats)

definitions.text: "Or emptied some dull — to the drains" (Keats)

blocks.clueFragment: "Or emptied some dull — to the drains"
blocks.note: a line from Keats's Ode to a Nightingale with one word missing
the source tells the solver to recall the poem and supply the missing word

explanation.walkthrough: The full line of Ode to a Nightingale reads 'Or emptied some dull OPIATE to the drains', describing a drowsy numbness.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats wrote this word in the gap, comparing his heavy numbness to having drained a sleep-inducing narcotic drug.

clue.text: A toady, though shy, can't possibly be out of work

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters could be arranged some other way than printed
to be out of something here means to lie around its outside, wrapping it

blocks.note: the two words taken letter by letter as raw material
OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A flatterer, however bashful, simply cannot afford to be unemployed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of work' reads as unemployed, but it means the shuffled letters sit outside the abbreviation for an opus.
explanation.definitionFit: A sycophant is a fawning flatterer who seeks favour, exactly what a toady is.

clue.text: Dr Jekyll's laboratory?

blocks.note: surface reading: the room where the scientist did his experiments
setter's reading: the place where he transformed into Mr Hyde, so a place for turning into someone else

explanation.walkthrough: Jekyll used his laboratory to change into Hyde; a CHANGING-ROOM is ordinarily where people swap their clothes, at a gym or sports ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Jekyll's lab was literally the chamber where he transformed, which the everyday name for a place to swap clothes describes.

clue.text: Port control and crime detection experts are unruffled

blocks.note: the Port of London Authority, which controlled London's docks
the Criminal Investigation Department, Britain's plain-clothes detective branch

explanation.surface: Harbour authorities and detectives keep their cool under pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: Placid describes someone calm and not easily upset, which is what unruffled means.

clue.text: Takes precedence on the housetops

definitions.note: a location phrase standing for a noun: the things found on the housetops

blocks.note: first meaning: goes first, is in front
second meaning: sheets of lead metal used to cover a roof

explanation.surface: Someone always insists on going first, even up on the rooftops.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means is ahead or in front; as a noun, British builders call lead roofing sheets this.

clue.text: Pluck is half the battle

blocks.note: surface reading: the proverb that courage gets you halfway to winning
setter's reading: a word for pick out or select makes up the first half of the name of a battle

explanation.walkthrough: CULL means pluck or pick out, and it is the first half of CULLODEN, the 1746 battle in Scotland where the Jacobites were crushed.
explanation.definitionFit: Culloden is the Scottish moor where the last pitched battle on British soil was fought in 1746.

clue.text: Spread for Pluto by himself

blocks.note: Dis is another Roman name for Pluto, god of the underworld
the Latin phrase per se means by itself

explanation.surface: A cartoon dog, left alone, goes looking for something to put on toast.
explanation.definitionFit: To disperse is to scatter or distribute widely, which is a meaning of the verb spread.

clue.text: Little girl meets Tom in Paris for small talk

blocks.note: a chit is an old word for a young or slight girl
chat is French for cat, so a tomcat in Paris

explanation.surface: A young girl encounters a man named Tom while in Paris and they make conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom' looks like a man's name, but here it is a tomcat, translated into French.
explanation.definitionFit: Chitchat is light, casual conversation, the same thing as small talk.

clue.text: Furs to suit Hamlet

definitions.note: a phrase pointing to Hamlet's own words, 'a suit of sables'

blocks.note: first meaning: pelts of the sable, a small dark-furred animal
second meaning: Hamlet says he will 'have a suit of ...', meaning black mourning clothes

explanation.surface: Fur garments chosen to fit the gloomy Danish prince.
explanation.definitionFit: Sables are costly animal pelts, and in old usage also black mourning garments, which Hamlet mentions wearing.

clue.text: Bolt of the runaway rider

blocks.note: surface reading: a horseman who flees, bolting away
setter's reading: an arrow loosed backwards by a retreating mounted archer of ancient Persia

explanation.walkthrough: Parthian horse archers pretended to flee and fired arrows behind them as they rode; a PARTHIAN SHOT is now any cutting remark made while leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Parthian cavalry fired arrows over their shoulders while retreating, the original sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Goes to pot in this bar

indicators.note: in this tells you the letters sit inside the words just printed

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word into the next two

explanation.surface: A drinking establishment that has been allowed to decline badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub in the surface, but it is the verb: in law, to ESTOP is to bar or prevent someone from asserting something.
explanation.definitionFit: Estop is a legal verb meaning to preclude or prevent a party from making a claim, so it means bar.

clue.text: The premier bagman

blocks.note: surface reading: the foremost travelling salesman or money collector
setter's reading: a Victorian prime minister who gave his name to a kind of hinged travelling bag

explanation.walkthrough: William GLADSTONE was British prime minister four times, and the Gladstone bag, a hinged leather travelling case, is named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: This prime minister lent his surname to a leather travelling bag, making him a premier connected to bags.

clue.text: Troupers, or troopers, with a rustic objective?

blocks.note: first sense: travelling actors touring rural areas

blocks.clueFragment: or troopers, with a rustic objective?
blocks.note: setter's reading: soldiers whose target is a farm building they charge at

explanation.surface: Touring actors, or soldiers attacking something in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnstormers were touring players who performed in barns; taken literally, soldiers storming a barn would be the same thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnstormers were itinerant theatrical performers touring country districts, which is what troupers are.

clue.text: Car Eleven needs change of bearing

indicators.note: a change of something alters its order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the two words taken letter by letter as raw material

explanation.surface: A racing car numbered eleven has to change direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change of bearing' reads like a new compass heading, but 'bearing' is the definition, as in 'has a bearing on'.
explanation.definitionFit: Relevance is connection to the matter in hand, the same sense as bearing in 'has some bearing on it'.

clue.text: Fatal frame-up

blocks.note: surface reading: a deadly false accusation
setter's reading: a wooden frame put up for executions

explanation.walkthrough: A frame-up usually means falsely incriminating someone; here it is a frame literally put up, the platform for a hanging.
explanation.definitionFit: A scaffold is the raised wooden platform built for public executions, a frame erected with deadly purpose.

clue.text: Dreadnought?

blocks.note: surface reading: a large early-twentieth-century battleship
setter's reading: split into two words, 'dread nought', meaning afraid of nothing

explanation.walkthrough: Split the battleship's name into 'dread nought' and you have an instruction to be afraid of nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who dreads nothing has no fear at all, which is the plain meaning of the adjective.

clue.text: Marion's charger heads all horses racing in Derbyshire

definitions.note: a location phrase standing for a place: a town in Derbyshire

blocks.note: in Scott's poem Marmion the dying hero cries 'Charge, Chester, charge!'; 'Marion' appears to be a misprint
the field is every horse running in a race

explanation.surface: A woman's warhorse leads the pack at a race meeting in the Derbyshire countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: Chester is the one Marmion orders to charge, so he is the charger. Chesterfield is a town in Derbyshire, a county in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Chesterfield is a market town in Derbyshire, famous for its crooked church spire.

clue.text: Worker from the Oriental Oil Co?

indicators.note: from suggests the letters are made out of, rebuilt from, what follows

blocks.note: E for east, the direction of the Orient
the words taken letter by letter as raw material

explanation.surface: A labourer employed by an Eastern oil company.
explanation.definitionFit: Coolie is an old, now offensive term for an unskilled hired labourer in Asia, so a worker.

clue.text: At five a girl is got up by slave

indicators.note: in a down clue, something got up is raised, so the letters read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: a lass is a girl
taken as written
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: At five o'clock a girl is dressed up by a servant.
explanation.definitionFit: A vassal was a feudal tenant bound in service to a lord, so a subordinate or slave.

clue.text: They were victimised if not passed over

definitions.text: They were victimised if not passed over

blocks.clueFragment: They were victimised if not passed over
blocks.note: surface reading: people who suffered because nobody ignored them
setter's reading: in Exodus the angel of death passed over marked houses and struck the eldest children in the rest

explanation.walkthrough: In the tenth plague of Egypt the eldest child of every household was killed unless the angel passed over the house, the origin of Passover.
explanation.definitionFit: The Exodus story says the eldest children of Egypt died in every home the angel of death did not skip.

clue.text: Piece of equipment one is supplied with on guard

indicators.note: being supplied with something here means swapping it in for the letter named

blocks.note: a thing is an item or piece of kit
I is the Roman numeral for one; this is the letter taken out
taken as written; this goes in its place

explanation.surface: A sentry is issued a piece of kit while on guard duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On guard' looks like a phrase, but 'on' is wordplay and 'guard' is the definition. The fit is loose: a thong is a strap, which can serve as a protective guard.
explanation.definitionFit: A thong is a narrow leather strap, and straps can act as guards or restraints, a loose and old-fashioned equivalence.

clue.text: Musical flower like Patience on a monument

definitions.note: an allusion standing for the character it describes

blocks.note: first meaning: a name shared by a stringed instrument and a garden flower related to the pansy
second meaning: the heroine of Twelfth Night, whose disguised speech describes a girl who 'sat like Patience on a monument'

explanation.surface: A flower in music is compared to the statue of a patient woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Viola in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night tells of a lovesick girl who 'sat like Patience on a monument, smiling at grief', really describing herself.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a stringed instrument, a pansy-like flower, and the Shakespeare heroine who speaks of Patience on a monument.

clue.text: The senior officer with the eastern bunch is a beast!

blocks.note: OC is the Officer Commanding
E abbreviates eastern
a lot is a group or set

explanation.surface: A commanding officer who sides with the Eastern faction is brutish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A beast' looks like an insult for the officer, but it is the definition: a wild animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocelot is a spotted wild cat of the Americas, so an animal or beast.

clue.text: Complaint of roof workers and hairdressers

definitions.note: names the trades for what they work with

blocks.note: first meaning: a painful viral illness producing a band of blisters
second meaning: wooden roof tiles, and short tapered haircuts fashionable in the 1920s

explanation.surface: A grievance shared by roofers and barbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' reads like a grumble, but here it is an illness. A shingle is a roof tile and also a short cropped hairstyle.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a viral illness, the thin tiles roofers lay, and the bobbed haircuts hairdressers gave.

clue.text: Same again, wise guy — it's what the doctor ordered

blocks.note: do is short for ditto, meaning the same again
a sage is a wise man

explanation.surface: A know-all orders another round, claiming it is on medical advice.
explanation.definitionFit: A dosage is the amount of medicine prescribed, which is literally what a doctor orders.

clue.text: Where the real appears a bit airy-fairy

indicators.note: a bit of the wording appears, so only part of the printed text is used

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word through the next two

explanation.surface: A philosophical remark that wherever reality shows up, it seems a little insubstantial.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethereal means delicate and insubstantial, not of the solid world, close to the colloquial airy-fairy.
